newsitem.title: GERMANY: Little market impact if IMF sells gold -S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Little market impact if IMF sells gold -S.Africa.

text.p: South Africa's central bank chief said on Friday that the International Monetary Fund would probably sell small parts of its gold reserves, but added this would not have a major effect on the gold market if it was done "in a responsible way".
Reserve Bank Governor Christian Stals said he expected the sales of gold to go ahead, telling a news conference in Frankfurt, "It looks like it (the IMF) is going to sell small parts of its gold."
But he said that the process would not have a "major effect" on the gold market given that annual production was already not sufficient to cover growing demand.

IMF management, backed by the U.S., Britain and most other member nations, has proposed selling around five million of the Fund's 104 million ounces of gold to help finance the stepped-up assistance to poor countries.
But Germany, Italy and Switzerland have opposed the proposal, arguing in part that the IMF should not sell gold except in cases of extreme financial emergency.

The IMF board was slated to meet on Friday to discuss ways to beef up its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility for poor nations and back a multilateral initiative to provide debt relief for some of the worst off countries as well.

As one of the world's major gold producers, South Africa had discouraged the IMF from selling gold, Stals said. But at the same time the country was sympathetic to the reason for doing so -- to fund aid for poor countries.
"It is difficult for us to say to the IMF we are against the idea," Stals noting that other African countries stood to benefit from the funds that gold sales would release.
But he urged the Fund to be cautious in the way in which it managed the sales. "Please if you have to sell gold, feed it slowly into the market, do it in a responsible way," he said.
Stals was speaking at a news conference as part of a European road show for prospective investors in a planned mark-denominated South African Eurobond, due to be issued shortly.
